purpose: Levonorgestrel is used to prevent pregnancy. It comes in two main forms: an emergency contraceptive pill (like Plan B) that you take after unprotected sex, and an intrauterine device (IUD) that provides long-term birth control for several years. It does NOT end an existing pregnancy — it works to prevent one from starting.
how_it_works: Levonorgestrel is a man-made version of the natural hormone progesterone, which your body already makes. It works mainly by stopping or delaying the release of an egg from your ovary so that sperm cannot fertilize it. It may also thicken the mucus in your cervix, making it harder for sperm to reach an egg.
common_side_effects: The most common side effects include nausea, headache, dizziness, tiredness, and breast tenderness. Your next menstrual period may come earlier or later than usual, or be heavier or lighter. Some people experience spotting or irregular bleeding, especially with the IUD form.
warnings: This medication does NOT protect against sexually transmitted infections (STIs). If you are already pregnant, this medication will not work and should not be used. Let your doctor know if you have unexplained vaginal bleeding, liver problems, or a history of blood clots. The emergency pill is most effective when taken as soon as possible — ideally within 72 hours of unprotected sex. If your period is more than a week late after taking the emergency pill, take a pregnancy test.
typical_dosing: For the emergency contraceptive pill (Plan B): Take one 1.5 mg tablet as soon as possible after unprotected sex, within 72 hours (3 days) — the sooner the better. For the IUD (Mirena, Kyleena, etc.): A healthcare provider inserts it into your uterus, and it can protect you for 3 to 8 years depending on the brand.
